title: Ephesians

stories.title: 📜 Ephesians 1
summaryBullets: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus: (1:1).
Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. (1:2).
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms. (1:3).
For He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence. In love (1:4).
He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will, (1:5).
to the praise of His glorious grace, which He has freely given us in the Beloved One. (1:6).
In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace (1:7).
that He lavished on us with all wisdom and understanding. (1:8).
And He has made known to us the mystery of His will according to His good pleasure, which He purposed in Christ (1:9).
as a plan for the fullness of time, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ. (1:10).
In Him we were also chosen as God’s own, having been predestined according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will, (1:11).
in order that we, who were the first to hope in Christ, would be for the praise of His glory. (1:12).
And in Him, having heard and believed the word of truth — the gospel of your salvation — you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, (1:13).
who is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God’s possession, to the praise of His glory. (1:14).
For this reason, ever since I heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints, (1:15).
I have not stopped giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, (1:16).
that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in your knowledge of Him. (1:17).
I ask that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened, so that you may know the hope of His calling, the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints, (1:18).
and the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe. These are in accordance with the working of His mighty strength, (1:19).
which He exerted in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms, (1:20).
far above all rule and authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in the present age but also in the one to come. (1:21).
And God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church, (1:22).
which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all. (1:23).
crossRefs: Romans 8:15-17: Adoption and inheritance.
2 Corinthians 1:21-22: God seals us with the Spirit.
Colossians 1:13-14: Redemption and forgiveness through Christ.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּן מְאֻמָּץ (ben meʾummāṣ, sense), Greek: υἱοθεσία (huiothesía, NT), Aramaic: אֻסְיָנָא (ʾusyānā)
translationNotes.note: Legal placement of a son into a family; Paul uses it for believers’ new status before God.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוֹד (sōd), Greek: μυστήριον (mystḗrion, NT), Aramaic: רָזָא (rāzā)
translationNotes.note: In Paul, not something unknowable but a divine plan once hidden and now revealed.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חוֹתָם (ḥōtām) / עֵרָבוֹן (ʿērāvon), Greek: σφραγίς (sphragís) / ἀρραβών (arrabṓn, NT), Aramaic: חותמא (ḥūṯāmā) / ערבון (ʿarāvōn)
translationNotes.note: Seal: mark of ownership or authenticity. Guarantee: pledge or down payment; the Spirit as first installment of full inheritance.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul greets the saints and declares blessings in Christ: election, adoption, redemption, revelation of God’s plan, inheritance, and sealing with the Spirit.

stories.title: 🌅 Ephesians 2
summaryBullets: And you were dead in your trespasses and sins, (2:1).
in which you used to walk when you conformed to the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience. (2:2).
All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath. (2:3).
But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, (2:4).
made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by grace you have been saved! (2:5).
And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, (2:6).
in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace, demonstrated by His kindness to us in Christ Jesus. (2:7).
For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, (2:8).
not by works, so that no one can boast. (2:9).
For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life. (2:10).
Therefore remember that formerly you who are Gentiles in the flesh and called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision (that done in the body by human hands) — (2:11).
remember that at that time you were separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world. (2:12).
But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ. (2:13).
For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility (2:14).
by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees. He did this to create in Himself one new man out of the two, thus making peace (2:15).
and reconciling both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which He put to death their hostility. (2:16).
He came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near. (2:17).
For through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit. (2:18).
Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, (2:19).
built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone. (2:20).
In Him the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. (2:21).
And in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit. (2:22).
crossRefs: Romans 5:8: God’s love shown while we were sinners.
Colossians 2:13: Made alive with Christ, forgiven of trespasses.
Titus 3:5: Saved not by works but by God’s mercy.

translationNotes.term: Ruler of the power of the air
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂר הָאֲוִיר (śar hāʾawîr, sense), Greek: ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος (archonta tēs exousías tou aéros, NT), Aramaic: שולטנא דהאוירא (shulṭānā d-hāwīrā)
translationNotes.note: Phrase for the spiritual ruler influencing disobedience; commonly understood as the devil or hostile spiritual power.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֵן (ḥēn), Greek: χάρις (cháris, NT), Aramaic: טיבותא (ṭîḇūṯā)
translationNotes.note: Favor or gift freely given; central to Paul’s description of salvation.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעֲשֶׂה (maʿăśeh), Greek: ποίημα (poíēma, NT), Aramaic: עובדא (ʿovdā)
translationNotes.note: Literally 'something made'; used of believers as God’s creation in Christ.

stories.keyTakeaway: Believers once dead in sin are made alive and exalted with Christ; salvation is by God’s grace through faith, not by works, and results in walking in good works prepared by God.

stories.title: 📜 Ephesians 3
summaryBullets: For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles... (3:1).
Surely you have heard about the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, (3:2).
that is, the mystery made known to me by revelation, as I have already written briefly. (3:3).
In reading this, then, you will be able to understand my insight into the mystery of Christ, (3:4).
which was not made known to men in other generations as it has now been revealed by the Spirit to God’s holy apostles and prophets. (3:5).
This mystery is that through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus. (3:6).
I became a servant of this gospel by the gift of God’s grace, given me through the working of His power. (3:7).
Though I am less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given me: to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, (3:8).
and to illuminate for everyone the stewardship of this mystery, which for ages past was kept hidden in God, who created all things. (3:9).
His purpose was that now, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God should be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms, (3:10).
according to the eternal purpose that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord. (3:11).
In Him and through faith in Him we may enter God’s presence with boldness and confidence. (3:12).
So I ask you not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory. (3:13).
... for this reason I bow my knees before the Father, (3:14).
from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name. (3:15).
I ask that out of the riches of His glory He may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being, (3:16).
so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith. Then you, being rooted and grounded in love, (3:17).
will have power, together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth (3:18).
of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. (3:19).
Now to Him who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine, according to His power that is at work within us, (3:20).
to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen. (3:21).
crossRefs: Colossians 1:26-27: The mystery revealed to the saints.
Romans 16:25-26: The mystery kept secret but now disclosed.
Acts 22:21: Paul sent to the Gentiles.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סוֹד (sōd), Greek: μυστήριον (mystḗrion, NT), Aramaic: רָזָא (rāzā)
translationNotes.note: Not unknowable but a divine plan once hidden and now revealed, especially concerning Gentile inclusion in Christ.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׂרִים וּשְׁלִיטִים (śārîm u-šelīṭîm, sense), Greek: ἀρχαί (archaí), ἐξουσίαι (exousíai, NT), Aramaic: רשותא (reshūtā), שלטן (shulṭān)
translationNotes.note: Terms for spiritual or cosmic powers; Paul emphasizes that God’s wisdom is displayed even to them through the church.

translationNotes.original: Greek: δέσμιος (desmios)
translationNotes.note: Paul is not speaking figuratively in 3:1 and 4:1. Acts 28:16 and 28:30-31 have him in Rome for two full years in a house he rented himself, guarded by a soldier and free to receive anyone who came and to preach without hindrance. He was chained to that soldier (Acts 28:20), which is the lighter arrangement a Roman citizen awaiting trial could be granted rather than a cell. Rome did not feed its prisoners, so his food, rent, and writing materials came from the churches (Philippians 4:14-18).

translationNotes.original: Greek: πατήρ (pater) - Greek: πατριά (patria)
translationNotes.note: Ephesians 3:14-15 is a play on words that English cannot carry. Pater is father; patria is the group that traces itself to one father, a clan or family line, and it is the ordinary word for the ancestral houses Israel was counted by (Numbers 1:2, Luke 2:4). Paul kneels to the pater from whom every patria takes its name. The two words are the same root, one sentence apart.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul explains his stewardship of God’s grace: the revealed mystery that Gentiles are fellow heirs in Christ, proclaimed through the gospel, showing God’s wisdom to heavenly powers.

stories.title: 🤝 Ephesians 4
summaryBullets: As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received: (4:1).
with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, (4:2).
and with diligence to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace. (4:3).
There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; (4:4).
one Lord, one faith, one baptism; (4:5).
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. (4:6).
Now to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. (4:7).
This is why it says: “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men.” (4:8).
What does “He ascended” mean, except that He also descended to the lower parts of the earth? (4:9).
He who descended is the very One who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things. (4:10).
And it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, (4:11).
to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ, (4:12).
until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God, as we mature to the full measure of the stature of Christ. (4:13).
Then we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching and by the clever cunning of men in their deceitful scheming. (4:14).
Instead, speaking the truth in love, we will in all things grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head. (4:15).
From Him the whole body, fitted and held together by every supporting ligament, grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part. (4:16).
So I tell you this, and insist on it in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking. (4:17).
They are darkened in their understanding and alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them due to the hardness of their hearts. (4:18).
Having lost all sense of shame, they have given themselves over to sensuality for the practice of every kind of impurity, with a craving for more. (4:19).
But this is not the way you came to know Christ. (4:20).
Surely you heard of Him and were taught in Him— in keeping with the truth that is in Jesus— (4:21).
to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires; (4:22).
to be renewed in the spirit of your minds; (4:23).
and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness. (4:24).
Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another. (4:25).
“Be angry, yet do not sin.” Do not let the sun set upon your anger, (4:26).
and do not give the devil a foothold. (4:27).
He who has been stealing must steal no longer, but must work, doing good with his own hands, that he may have something to share with the one in need. (4:28).
Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen. (4:29).
And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. (4:30).
Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice. (4:31).
Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you. (4:32).
crossRefs: 1 Corinthians 12:4-7: Varieties of gifts but one Spirit.
Psalm 68:18: Ascending on high and giving gifts.
Colossians 1:18: Christ as head of the body.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עָלָה / יָרַד (ʿālāh / yārad), Greek: ἀνέβη (anébē) / κατέβη (katébē, NT), Aramaic: סליק (seliq) / נחת (naḥat)
translationNotes.note: Common verbs for going up or down; Paul applies them to Christ’s descent and exaltation.

translationNotes.term: He led captives away and gave gifts
translationNotes.original: Greek: αἰχμαλωσία (aichmalosia)
translationNotes.note: Ephesians 4:8 quotes Psalm 68:18, and the scene is a victory procession: the winner comes up in front of his people with the prisoners walking ahead of him, and then the plunder is shared out. Sharing the spoil was a fixed part of ancient war. Numbers 31:25-30 sets how plunder was divided between the fighters and the rest of the congregation, and David sent shares of Amalekite spoil to the elders of Judah after Ziklag (1 Samuel 30:26-31).

translationNotes.original: Greek: ποιμήν (poimen) - Greek: εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistes)
translationNotes.note: Both words in 4:11 are ordinary job descriptions rather than church titles. Poimen means shepherd, a man who lived with the flock, led it to water, and fought off predators, which is the picture Jesus uses in John 10:11-15 and Ezekiel 34 uses of Israel's rulers. Euangelistes is built from the word for good news and means a man who carries an announcement; Philip carries that description in Acts 21:8. Neither word appears in English as what it actually says.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֶרֶב (erev) - Greek: παροργισμός (parorgismos)
translationNotes.note: The deadline in 4:26 is sharper than it looks in English, because the Hebrew day begins at sunset, not at midnight (Genesis 1:5, Leviticus 23:32). Letting the sun go down on anger means carrying it into the next day. The first half of the verse quotes Psalm 4:4 as the Greek Old Testament reads it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul calls for unity in the Spirit and explains that Christ gives diverse gifts to equip and grow the church into maturity as his body.

stories.title: 🌟 Ephesians 5
summaryBullets: Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, (5:1).
and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God. (5:2).
But among you, as is proper among the saints, there must not be even a hint of sexual immorality, or of any kind of impurity, or of greed. (5:3).
Nor should there be obscenity, foolish talk, or crude joking, which are out of character, but rather thanksgiving. (5:4).
For of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. (5:5).
Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience. (5:6).
Therefore do not be partakers with them. (5:7).
For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, (5:8).
for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth. (5:9).
Test and prove what pleases the Lord. (5:10).
Have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness, but rather expose them. (5:11).
For it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret. (5:12).
But everything exposed by the light becomes visible, for everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself. (5:13).
So it is said: “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” (5:14).
Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, (5:15).
redeeming the time, because the days are evil. (5:16).
Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is. (5:17).
Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit. (5:18).
Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord, (5:19).
always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. (5:20).
Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. (5:21).
Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord. (5:22).
For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior. (5:23).
Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything. (5:24).
Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her (5:25).
to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, (5:26).
and to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless. (5:27).
In the same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. (5:28).
Indeed, no one ever hated his own body, but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church. (5:29).
For we are members of His body. (5:30).
“For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” (5:31).
This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church. (5:32).
Nevertheless, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband. (5:33).
crossRefs: Colossians 3:18-19: The same pair of instructions in Paul's other letter, where husbands are told to love their wives and not to be harsh with them.
Genesis 2:24: The verse Paul quotes at 5:31, that a man leaves his father and mother, is united to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
1 Peter 3:7: Husbands are to treat their wives with consideration and honour them as fellow heirs of the gift of life, with their own prayers hindered if they do not.
Colossians 3:16-17: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs sung with thankfulness, the parallel to 5:18-20.
John 8:12: Jesus says 'I am the light of the world', the light 5:8-14 tells the reader they now walk as children of.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: זְנוּת (zenût), Greek: πορνεία (porneía, NT), Aramaic: זנותא (zenūtā)
translationNotes.note: Refers to unlawful sexual activity; Paul lists it among sins barring inheritance in God’s kingdom.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּנֵי אוֹר (bənē ʾôr), Greek: τέκνα φωτός (tékna phōtós, NT), Aramaic: בני נהורא (bnay nehôrā)
translationNotes.note: Figurative expression for those transformed by Christ, living in truth and holiness.

translationNotes.term: Do not get drunk on wine
translationNotes.original: Greek: οἶνος (oinos) - Greek: ἄκρατος (akratos)
translationNotes.note: Wine in the ancient Mediterranean was normally cut with water before it was drunk, commonly one part wine to two or three of water, and drinking it neat was treated as the mark of a barbarian or a drunk. Getting drunk therefore took deliberate effort. Ecstatic drunkenness was also the recognised form of some pagan worship, above all the rites of Dionysus, which is the contrast standing behind 5:18: not filled with wine, but filled with the Spirit.

Instructions to a household were a standard form in the ancient world, and Aristotle sets out the pattern in Politics 1.1253b: the household is the man's to rule, and the discussion is about how he should govern his wife, his children, and his slaves. The Roman head of a house, the paterfamilias, held legal authority over his children for life and owned the slaves outright. What is unusual in 5:21-6:9 and Colossians 3:18-4:1 is that the subordinate parties are addressed directly, as people who can be spoken to and can answer, and that the man is given commands of his own rather than advice on management.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ὑποτασσόμενοι (hypotassomenoi)
translationNotes.note: In Greek 5:18-22 is a single sentence. 'Be filled with the Spirit' is the command, and everything after it hangs off that command as participles: speaking, singing, giving thanks, and submitting to one another (5:21). The oldest copies of the letter, the papyrus P46 from about AD 200 and Codex Vaticanus, carry no verb at all in 5:22; the line there reads 'wives, to your own husbands, as to the Lord', and the verb has to be carried down from 5:21. English cannot leave a sentence without a verb, so translations supply one, and supplying it starts a new sentence where the Greek has none.

translationNotes.term: What the husband is told to do
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀγαπάω (agapao) - παραδίδωμι (paradidomi)
translationNotes.note: The wife's instruction runs three verses, 5:22-24. The husband's runs nine, 5:25-33, and the standard set for him is Christ giving Himself up for the church: the verb at 5:25 is paradidomi, to hand over, the same verb the Gospels use of Jesus being handed over to be crucified. He is told to love her as his own body (5:28-29), and the section ends with the command repeated a fourth time at 5:33.

stories.keyTakeaway: Believers must walk in love, light, and wisdom, avoiding impurity and idolatry, filled with the Spirit in worship and mutual submission.

stories.title: 🏠 Ephesians 6
summaryBullets: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. (6:1).
“Honor your father and mother” (which is the first commandment with a promise), (6:2).
“that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth.” (6:3).
Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. (6:4).
Slaves, obey your earthly masters with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ. (6:5).
And do this not only to please them while they are watching, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from your heart. (6:6).
Serve with good will, as to the Lord and not to men, (6:7).
because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does, whether he is slave or free. (6:8).
And masters, do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him. (6:9).
Finally, be strong in the Lord and in His mighty power. (6:10).
Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil’s schemes. (6:11).

For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. (6:12).
Therefore take up the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you will be able to stand your ground, and having done everything, to stand. (6:13).
Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness arrayed, (6:14).
and with your feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace. (6:15).
In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. (6:16).
And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. (6:17).
Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition. To this end, stay alert with all perseverance in your prayers for all the saints. (6:18).
Pray also for me, that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, (6:19).
for which I am an ambassador in chains. Pray that I may proclaim it fearlessly, as I should. (6:20).
Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will tell you everything, so that you also may know about me and what I am doing. (6:21).
I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts. (6:22).
Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. (6:23).
Grace to all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love. (6:24).
crossRefs: Colossians 3:22-4:1: The same instruction to slaves and masters, ending with the order that masters supply their slaves with what is right and fair because they too have a Master in heaven.
1 Timothy 1:9-10: Paul lists slave traders, andrapodistai, in the same breath as murderers and perjurers among those the law is enacted against.
Deuteronomy 23:15-16: A runaway slave must not be handed back to his master but may settle in any town he chooses, the reverse of every surrounding law code.
Philemon 1:15-16: Paul sends Onesimus back to his owner and asks that he be received 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother'.
Exodus 20:12: 'Honor your father and mother', the commandment Paul quotes at 6:2 and calls the first one with a promise attached.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִכְנִיעַ (hiknîaʿ, sense), Greek: ὑποτάσσω (hypotássō, NT), Aramaic: אשתעבד (ʾištʿābed)
translationNotes.note: Verb for arranging under or yielding; used for voluntary order in relationships.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (bāśār ʾeḥād), Greek: σὰρξ μία (sarx mía, NT), Aramaic: בשר חד (beśar ḥad)
translationNotes.note: Phrase from Genesis 2:24 describing marital union.

translationNotes.original: Greek: δοῦλος (doulos) - ἀνδραποδιστής (andrapodistes)
translationNotes.note: A doulos was owned outright. Roman law counted him property, bought and sold and punished at the owner's discretion, with no standing to bring a case. What is unusual here comes at verse 9, which turns and gives the owner orders: do the same for them, give up your use of threats, because the One who is both their Master and yours is in heaven and shows no favouritism. Paul lists andrapodistai, slave traders, with murderers and perjurers at 1 Timothy 1:10, the same crime the Torah makes capital at Exodus 21:16 and Deuteronomy 24:7, and he asks Philemon to take Onesimus back 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother' (Philemon 1:16).

translationNotes.original: Greek: περιζώννυμι (perizonnymi) - Hebrew: חָגַר (chagar)
translationNotes.note: The belt goes on first because everything else hangs on it. A Roman soldier's belt was the badge of service, carried the sword, and gathered the tunic so it did not catch the legs. The Hebrew idiom behind it is girding up the loins: pulling a long robe up through the belt so a man can run or fight. Israel ate the first Passover that way, belt fastened and sandals on (Exodus 12:11), and Elijah tucked his cloak into his belt and outran Ahab's chariot to Jezreel (1 Kings 18:46).

translationNotes.original: Greek: θώραξ (thorax)
translationNotes.note: First-century legionaries wore either a shirt of interlinked iron rings or the banded plate armour that came into use in that century, and either one weighed twenty pounds or more and covered a man from shoulders to hips. It protected the trunk and nothing else, so it was worn where a wound kills. Isaiah 59:17 has the LORD putting on righteousness as a breastplate, which is the line 6:14 is picking up.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ὑποδέομαι (hypodeomai)
translationNotes.note: The Roman army marched on the caliga, a heavy open boot with a thick sole studded with iron hobnails, which gripped ground and lasted under a legion's mileage; the emperor Gaius got the nickname Caligula, little boot, as a child in his father's camp. Footwear is what makes an army mobile, and the word in 6:15 is about being ready to move. Isaiah 52:7 is behind the phrase, where feet carry good news over the mountains.

translationNotes.original: Greek: θυρεός (thyreos) - Greek: θύρα (thyra)
translationNotes.note: The Greek word in 6:16 is not the small round shield but the big one, and the word says so: thyreos comes from thyra, a door, because it was door-shaped and covered the man. The Roman version was curved plywood faced with leather and hide, with an iron boss at the centre, and ranks locked them edge to edge into a wall. Leather facing is also why the fire arrows matter: burning shafts were shot to set equipment alight, and a soaked leather face put them out instead of catching.

translationNotes.original: Greek: περικεφαλαία (perikephalaia) - Greek: μάχαιρα (machaira) - Greek: ῥῆμα (rhema)
translationNotes.note: The helmet was iron or bronze with hinged cheek pieces and a flared neck guard, worn over padding, and it is the only piece in the list a man could not put on himself in a hurry. Isaiah 59:17 again supplies the image, a helmet of salvation. The sword is the machaira, the short blade of about twenty inches that Roman infantry used for stabbing at close quarters in formation rather than swinging. The word Paul uses for the word of God in 6:17 is rhema, a thing spoken, not the written volume.

translationNotes.original: Greek: Ἄρτεμις (Artemis)
translationNotes.note: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was counted one of the seven wonders of the world; Pliny the Elder gives it 425 feet by 225 with 127 columns sixty feet high (Natural History 36.95). The city lived off it. Silversmiths sold miniature shrines to pilgrims, and when Paul's preaching cut into that trade the craftsmen started a riot and filled the theatre, which held some twenty-four thousand people (Acts 19:23-41). Ephesus was also known across the empire for written magic spells, and Acts 19:19 says converts burned their books, valued at fifty thousand drachmas, which is fifty thousand days of a labourer's wages (Matthew 20:2).

stories.keyTakeaway: Paul instructs wives, husbands, children, parents, bondservants, and masters on relationships patterned after Christ’s love and authority.

intro:
Ephesians was written by Paul the apostle (Ephesians 1:1), one of the four "prison epistles" (along with Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon) Paul composed during his first Roman imprisonment of AD 60-62, when he was under house arrest in Rome awaiting trial before Nero on the appeal he had made as a Roman citizen (Acts 28:16-31). Paul mentions his imprisonment four times within the letter (Ephesians 3:1; 4:1; 6:20: "I am an ambassador in chains"). The letter was carried to its destination by Tychicus (Ephesians 6:21-22: "Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything... I have sent him to you for this very purpose"), a native of the Roman province of Asia (Acts 20:4) who served as Paul's trusted courier. Tychicus carried Ephesians on the same journey as the letter to the Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9) and the letter to Philemon, all three letters dispatched together from Rome and delivered through the cities of western Asia Minor. The phrase "in Ephesus" at Ephesians 1:1 is absent from the earliest surviving manuscripts (Papyrus 46 c. AD 175-225, Codex Sinaiticus, and Codex Vaticanus, all of which have a blank where the city name should appear), and the second-century writer Marcion (c. AD 140) referred to the letter as the epistle "to the Laodiceans." Most traditional commentators have concluded that Ephesians was originally a circular letter intended for multiple churches in the Roman province of Asia, with Ephesus serving as the lead congregation; Tychicus likely filled in the destination at each city as he delivered copies. The letter to the Laodiceans Paul mentions at Colossians 4:16 ("After this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea") may have been the same circular Ephesian letter at one stage of its delivery. Paul (originally Saul) was born in Tarsus of Cilicia around AD 5-10 to a Hebrew family of the tribe of Benjamin, educated in Jerusalem under Gamaliel the Pharisee before his conversion on the Damascus road and his apostolic ministry to the Gentiles; he was martyred by beheading in Rome under Nero around AD 66-67 (see the introduction to Romans for the full biographical sketch).

The historical setting is the city of Ephesus and the province of Asia in the early 60s AD, with Paul writing from his Roman house arrest. Ephesus was the largest city of Asia Minor and the third or fourth largest city of the Roman Empire (population estimates range from 200,000 to 250,000), serving as the political capital of the senatorial province of Asia and the religious center of the cult of Artemis (Roman Diana). The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, four times the size of the Athenian Parthenon, with 127 marble columns sixty feet high; pilgrims from across the empire came to worship Artemis and to purchase silver shrines as votive offerings, a trade that brought enormous wealth to Ephesian silversmiths and that triggered the riot against Paul recorded in Acts 19:23-41 when Paul's ministry threatened the cult's commerce. Paul had ministered in Ephesus for approximately three years on his third missionary journey (Acts 19, c. AD 53-56), the longest sustained ministry of his career, teaching daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus and seeing extraordinary spiritual results (the burning of magic books worth fifty thousand drachmas at Acts 19:18-19, the equivalent of fifty thousand days' wages for a laborer). Other figures from the New Testament associated with Ephesus include Priscilla and Aquila (who had moved from Corinth and instructed the eloquent Alexandrian Apollos there, Acts 18:18-26), Timothy (whom Paul later left in Ephesus to oversee the church, 1 Timothy 1:3), and the apostle John (who relocated to Ephesus after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 and ministered there until his death around AD 100).

Ephesians is the forty-ninth book of the Christian Bible, the tenth book of the New Testament, and the fifth of Paul's thirteen letters in canonical order. The letter has six chapters and is the first of the four prison epistles. The earliest surviving manuscript is Papyrus 46 (P46, c. AD 175-225), which contains Ephesians on the same Pauline codex as the rest of the corpus; other early witnesses include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). Several of Ephesians' passages have become foundational to Christian theology and practice: Ephesians 2:8-9 ("For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast") is one of the clearest New Testament statements of salvation by grace through faith; Ephesians 4:11-13 lists the fivefold equipping ministries given to the church (apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers); Ephesians 5:22-33 presents Christian marriage as a reflection of the relationship between Christ and the church; and Ephesians 6:10-18 is the famous "armor of God" passage (the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the gospel of peace as shoes, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit).
